newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul seeks talks with Pyongyang to defuse tension.
newsitem.headline: Seoul seeks talks with Pyongyang to defuse tension.

text.p: South Korea on Monday braced itself for possible attacks by North Korea but said it would seek a dialogue to defuse rising tensions after a high-level Pyongyang official sought asylum at Seoul's embassy in Beijing.
Another prominent defectior, Li Il-nam, a nephew of North Korean leader Kim Jong-il's ex-wife, was shot and critically wounded at the weekend by suspected North Korean agents near Seoul.
Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha said a diplomatic deadlock over the defection in Beijing last week by Hwang Jang-yop was just a start of headaches for Seoul because of a crisis in the North.

"I believe the North Korean regime's crisis will deepen as time passes because there's no likelihood of improvement in its economic hardship and food shortages, and signs of laxity in its social order," Yoo told a meeting of South Korean diplomats.

South Korea's security-related ministers on Sunday agreed that a desperate North Korea could stage terrorist attacks after Hwang, a top adviser to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il and Pyongyang's chief ideologue, sought asylum on Wednesday.
About 10,000 police and military troops searched for the two suspected North Korean agents who shot Li late on Saturday.

"We have drawn up a list of defectors, senior officials and politicians to provide tight security against any possible terrorist attacks by North Korea," a police officer told Reuters. "Security around ports, airports and other public places has also been beefed up."
The precautionary steps were taken after Home Affairs Minister Suh Chung-hwa denounced the shooting of Li as "an assassination attempt by North Korean infiltrators".
Seoul officials said Li, known in South Korea as Lee Han-yong, remained in a coma and was on a life support system on Monday in a hospital in Bundang, just south of Seoul.
Foreign Minister Yoo said Seoul, while increasing precautions against attack, would step up efforts to hold peace talks with North Korea, along with the United States and China.
"To manage the fluid situation on the Korean peninsula... and maintain peace, we should achieve four-nation peace talks," he said.
The talks, proposed jointly last year by Seoul and Washington, could discuss steps to reduce tensions on the divided peninsula and economic and other cooperation, he said.
In Beijing, Hwang spent his 74th birthday on Monday at the South Korean mission in Beijing behind a fortress-like defence wall provided by Chinese security officials.
Pyongyang has said Hwang was kidnapped by Seoul, a claim brushed aside as "preposterous" by South Korea.
"If the South uses force to move him to South Korea we will respond with force," said one Pyongyang diplomat keeping watch outside the South Korean consular office in Beijing.
South Korea's Foreign Ministry on Monday denied reports Hwang had met a U.S. intelligence official and revealed plans by other Northern officials to flee.
"No U.S. official has met Hwang Jang-yop," ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung said.

The state radio and local newspapers reported on Monday that Hwang had told an official from the U.S Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) that six to seven officials of North Korea's ruling Workers' Party wanted to seek political asylum.
"The news reports are not true at all," Lee said.
The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, Bill Richardson, said on Sunday Washington was closely watching developments involving North Korean defectors after the attack on Li.
"This is an incident that is serious," Richardson said on ABC Television's "This Week" programme. "This is an incident that we're watching very closely."
Richardson said U.S. intelligence analysts doubted North Korea was on the verge of collapse but were closely monitoring developments in the economically backward communist country.
